newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left denies NATO differences with Chirac.
newsitem.headline: French left denies NATO differences with Chirac.

text.p: France's ruling Socialists denied on Sunday any differences with Gaullist President Jacques Chirac on freezing the country's proposed return to the military wing of NATO at the alliance's Madrid summit meeting next month.

"Regarding the NATO summit, the president and the government make the same assessment of the situation...The conditions do not allow us to go any further," Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine told Europe 1 radio.
The left-wing government said last week the time was not ripe for France to return to NATO's military wing as Paris had not won the concessions it was seeking from Washington.
The president's office let it promptly know that Chirac felt there was still room for progress on NATO reform and he planned to keep all his options open ahead of the key Madrid meeting.
Some media saw this as an indication that the government had infringed constitutional practice giving the president the upper hand in foreign policy and defence matters.
Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has shared power with the conservative Chirac in an uneasy "cohabitation" since the left won a parliamentary election on June 1.

Socialist Jack Lang, the chairman of the National Assembly's Foreign Affairs Committee, also denied any differences but made it clear that the Socialist-led government would not be idle on foreign policy.
"Deciding on foreign policy belongs to the president and the prime minister. I do not think there has been any dispute," he tolr RTL radio.

He said it was only normal that Chirac, who proposed a full return to NATO 18 months ago, should keep handling the negotiations and Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin would not attend the Madrid summit.
"It is clear that in Madrid the president will have to state that the conditions for full reintegration (into NATO) have not been met," he said.
General de Gaulle pulled France out of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in 1966, accusing the alliance of being dominated by Washington.

As a condition for a return to full NATO participation, Chirac had demanded that the United States hand over to a European officer NATO's southern command, the Naples-based AFSOUTH which includes the U.S. Mediterranean Sixth Fleet.
Washington, which also runs NATO's supreme command based in Belgium, has rejected the French condition, saying this month it had stopped trying to resolve the long-running dispute.
Washington and Paris are also at odds over the alliance's plans to invite formerly Communist eastern European countries at the Madrid summit to join the alliance.
The United States wants only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to be asked to join, while France supports a broader enlargement including Slovenia and Romania.
